title: The Return

jokes.text: Dwight's resume breakdown: 'professional resume, athletic and special skills resume, and Dwight Schrute trivia'
jokes.setup: Dwight announces he has conveniently broken down his job search materials for the viewer's benefit
jokes.punchline: The third category is a vanity section literally called 'Dwight Schrute trivia' — as if prospective employers need a trivia sheet about him
jokes.explanation: Quintessentially Dwight: the grandiose self-regard, the pseudo-professional structure applied to something absurd. 'Dwight Schrute trivia' as a resume category is a perfect encapsulation of his narcissism without any additional explanation needed. Character integration is extremely high — only Dwight would do this.

jokes.text: How would I describe myself? Three words: hardworking, alpha male, jackhammer. Merciless. Insatiable.
jokes.setup: Dwight says he'll describe himself in 'three words'
jokes.punchline: He lists five items, including 'jackhammer,' 'merciless,' and 'insatiable' — none of which are words a normal person uses to describe themselves professionally, and he blows past the three-word constraint without acknowledgment
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes and earns its high score. The joke works on multiple levels simultaneously: the 'three words' setup is violated immediately (a classic Dwight obliviousness gag), the words themselves escalate from plausible to bizarre ('hardworking' to 'jackhammer' to 'insatiable'), and each new word is funnier than the last. 'Jackhammer' as a self-descriptor is both violent and sexually suggestive in a way Dwight probably doesn't intend — or maybe does — which is perfect ambiguity. Highly quotable, character-specific, and economical. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: 'There's nothing on my horizon except everything. Everything is on my horizon.'
jokes.setup: Dwight attempts a grand, inspiring closing statement about his future
jokes.punchline: He contradicts himself in consecutive sentences and seems to realize it mid-sentence, then doubles down rather than correcting
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Dwight is so committed to sounding powerful that he doesn't notice he's said two opposite things. The self-correction that isn't really a correction is very Dwight. Slightly less punchy than the surrounding jokes in this cold open.

jokes.text: Andy has recorded all four parts of 'Rockin' Robin' himself on his computer and set it as his ringtone
jokes.setup: A cheerful song plays; Jim (or a coworker) asks if that's Andy singing
jokes.punchline: Andy confirms he recorded all four vocal parts himself on his computer and it 'took forever' — the effort-to-payoff ratio is absurd and reveals his desperate need for attention and approval
jokes.explanation: Excellent character establishment for Andy. The detail of recording all four parts himself — not just downloading a ringtone but putting in significant personal labor to create it — perfectly encapsulates his exhausting try-hard energy. 'Took me forever' is the killer detail. High character integration because this behavior is uniquely Andy-ish.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I called it myself. Just thought you'd get a kick out of the new ring.'
jokes.setup: Andy's phone rings with his custom four-part harmony ringtone
jokes.punchline: He called his own phone to show it off to Jim — the performance wasn't spontaneous, it was staged for an audience of one
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I recorded all four parts' to 'I called myself to make you listen to it' is a perfect escalation of Andy's pathology. Each revelation makes him simultaneously more pitiable and more insufferable. Rewatch bonus because the setup makes the callback land harder.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I'd just like to say I'm thrilled to be working directly beneath you. I feel I have a lot to learn from you, even though you are younger and have less experience.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to ingratiate himself with Jim
jokes.punchline: The compliment completely undercuts itself — he explicitly notes Jim is younger and less experienced, making the 'compliment' a passive-aggressive non-compliment delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic cringe comedy — Andy is obliviously insulting Jim while trying to flatter him. The joke works because Andy means every word sincerely and doesn't register the contradiction. The line 'even though you are younger and have less experience' is the gem; it's the thing you're not supposed to say out loud in a compliment.

jokes.text: Andy's toast: 'Andy and the Tuna.'
jokes.setup: Andy is toasting to his new partnership with Jim (whom he calls 'Large Tuna')
jokes.punchline: The nickname 'Andy and the Tuna' frames their dynamic as a buddy duo that only Andy has signed up for — and Jim's visible discomfort (inferred) is the real punchline
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe beat. The unilateral declaration of a partnership name is very Andy, and 'the Tuna' as Jim's designated half of the duo lands because it's so bad. The joke is more setup for the ongoing Andy-Jim dynamic than a punchline in itself.

jokes.text: Jim's reaction beat: silent stare at the camera after 'Andy and the Tuna'
jokes.setup: Andy delivers his toast with complete self-satisfaction
jokes.punchline: Jim looks directly into the documentary camera with an expression of hollow despair — the look that says 'you see what I'm dealing with'
jokes.explanation: The Jim camera look is an Office institution. In the post-Dwight world, with Andy filling the 'insufferable desk neighbor' role, this beat efficiently communicates Jim's resignation and the audience's shared exasperation. Economy score is very high because a look does the work of a paragraph. The look is less devastating than the iconic Dwight-related camera looks, but still earns its place.

jokes.text: Jim confessional: 'I miss Dwight.'
jokes.setup: Throughout the series, Jim and Dwight have been antagonists; Jim has pranked Dwight relentlessly
jokes.punchline: Now that Dwight has been replaced by Andy — someone even more insufferable in a different way — Jim finds himself genuinely missing Dwight; three words deliver the entire thesis
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke and one of the series' most elegant moments. Three words that pay off seasons of Jim-Dwight antagonism in a way that's funny, poignant, and structurally perfect. It works as a standalone laugh, as a character revelation, and as a thematic statement about the episode. The economy score is a 10 — no joke in the episode achieves more with fewer words. Highly quotable, genuinely surprising yet inevitable in retrospect. This is comparable to an 8.5-9 on the anchor scale.

jokes.text: Jim confessional: 'Congratulations, universe. You win.'
jokes.setup: Jim has just admitted he misses Dwight; the confession itself is humiliating for him
jokes.punchline: Rather than accept this gracefully, Jim declares defeat to the abstract concept of the universe — framing his mild workplace irritation as a cosmic battle he has lost
jokes.explanation: Excellent extension of the 'I miss Dwight' beat. The grandiosity of 'Congratulations, universe. You win.' applied to something so petty is perfectly calibrated Jim Halpert humor — self-aware, sardonic, and deeply funny. Highly quotable and works as a standalone line even out of context. Just below an 8 on the anchor scale because it depends on the preceding beat.

jokes.text: Michael: 'How was your gay-cation?' then immediately: 'I thought of that like two seconds after you left.'
jokes.setup: Oscar returns to the office after a paid leave; Michael greets him in front of everyone
jokes.punchline: Michael has been holding onto this pun since Oscar left and cannot contain his pride in it — then admits he thought of it 'two seconds after you left,' meaning he's been sitting on 'gay-cation' for months waiting for this moment
jokes.explanation: The pun itself is cringe-worthy, which is the point — Michael thinks it's brilliant. But the real joke is the admission that he thought of it immediately after Oscar left and has been mentally rehearsing this delivery for months. That's deeply pathetic and deeply Michael. The character integration is very high: only Michael Scott would be this proud of this pun for this long.

jokes.text: Michael on Dwight leaving: 'Addition by subtraction.' Oscar: 'What does that even mean? That is impossible.'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to sound shrewd about Dwight's departure using business jargon
jokes.punchline: Oscar immediately and correctly identifies that the phrase is mathematically nonsensical; Michael's response is essentially 'yeah, you're right' before pivoting
jokes.explanation: Efficient joke: Michael deploys pseudo-wisdom, gets immediately and correctly called out, and concedes without embarrassment. The follow-up 'Addition by addition' for Oscar's return is a nice self-aware escalation. Works well but isn't exceptional.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Addition by subtraction' / 'Addition by addition' pairing for Dwight leaving and Oscar returning
jokes.setup: Michael is summarizing two personnel changes
jokes.punchline: He uses parallel but opposite nonsense formulas as if they are profundities, fully satisfied with his own rhetorical symmetry
jokes.explanation: The pairing is a moderate callback payoff. Michael's self-satisfaction in his own wordplay is in character, but the joke doesn't quite land as its own moment — it's more of a structural feature of the preceding exchange.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I thought of that like two seconds after you left.' — revealing he has been waiting three months to use this pun
jokes.setup: 'Gay-cation' gets a forced 'That's very funny' from Oscar
jokes.punchline: Michael reveals he has been holding onto this pun since Oscar's departure — he has been anticipating this moment for months
jokes.explanation: This is the better of the two jokes in this sequence. The implication — that Michael has been eagerly anticipating Oscar's return specifically to deploy this pun — reveals a pathetic, lovable quality. The three-month anticipation for a mediocre pun is deeply human and deeply Michael. It earns the 8+ because it requires no exaggeration; Michael would absolutely do this.

jokes.text: Angela's greeting to Oscar: a cold, clipped 'Oscar.' Nothing more.
jokes.setup: Various people are warmly welcoming Oscar back to the office
jokes.punchline: Angela's 'welcome back' is a single word — his name — delivered as if she is identifying an object rather than greeting a human being
jokes.explanation: Classic Angela economy. The contrast between everyone else's warmth and her flat acknowledgment is perfect character comedy. High economy score — saying only someone's name as a 'greeting' communicates everything about her character. Requires knowledge of Angela to fully land.

jokes.text: Andy's forced casual conversation with Jim: 'TGI Wednesday. Am I right?'
jokes.setup: Andy is aggressively attempting to bond with Jim through small talk
jokes.punchline: He applies the 'TGI Friday' celebratory format to Wednesday — a day nobody is happy about — with complete confidence that this is charming
jokes.explanation: Solidly funny because it's so effortful and so wrong. The specific wrongness of choosing Wednesday — the worst possible day to apply this format — and Andy's confidence is classic try-hard comedy. Not exceptional but a reliable chuckle.

jokes.text: Andy's itinerary: 'Gonna go home, get my beer on, get my Lost on.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to present himself as a relatable, cool guy with fun evening plans
jokes.punchline: His idea of a wild Wednesday night is beer and network TV — delivered with the energy of a man describing skydiving
jokes.explanation: The 'get my X on' construction is mildly funny but not especially original. Works as character texture — Andy trying to seem hip — but doesn't land a strong punch.

jokes.text: Andy invites Jim to hang out; Jim gives a non-committal 'maybe'; Andy: 'I'll take that as a maybe.'
jokes.setup: Andy floats a hangout invitation hoping for enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Jim says literally 'maybe' — the least enthusiastic possible response — and Andy repeats it back as if this is a positive development, framing the obvious rejection as an invitation to continue pursuing
jokes.explanation: Competent cringe beat. The joke is in Andy's complete inability to read social signals — treating 'maybe' as encouragement is a mild but effective character moment.

jokes.text: Andy follows Jim to the bathroom by announcing he's going to the kitchen and offering to 'walk with' him
jokes.setup: Jim tries to escape Andy by going to the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately announces he's also going somewhere adjacent and offers to accompany Jim — the non sequitur of 'I'll walk with you' to the bathroom is both socially wrong and completely serious
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of Andy's boundary-blindness. Walking someone to the bathroom as if it's a social activity is a genuinely uncomfortable premise executed efficiently.

jokes.text: Andy confessional: 'Things are going pretty good. Getting a lot of face time with the boss.'
jokes.setup: Andy reports on his workplace strategy as if executing a professional networking plan
jokes.punchline: Everything we've seen shows that Michael finds Andy deeply annoying — Andy's self-assessment is completely disconnected from reality, and his satisfaction in 'face time with the boss' recontextualizes all his painful sycophancy as deliberate strategy
jokes.explanation: Effective dramatic irony — Andy thinks he's executing a career strategy while the audience knows Michael finds him unsettling. The gap between his confidence and reality is classic Office comedy.

jokes.text: Michael asks Oscar to join the party planning committee. Oscar: 'The committee with all the women?' Michael: 'Yeah.' Oscar: 'Because I'm gay.' Michael: 'No, no—'
jokes.setup: Michael tries to make an inclusive gesture toward Oscar
jokes.punchline: Oscar immediately and correctly identifies the actual reasoning behind the invitation; Michael's denial and subsequent stammering about 'certain events' confirms Oscar's read
jokes.explanation: Excellent character exchange. Oscar's blunt 'Because I'm gay' strips away Michael's attempt at progressive posturing, and Michael's inability to deny it with any coherence is perfectly in character. The sequence of 'certain events...certain things...certain situations...certain accountants' is a great escalating evasion.

jokes.text: Michael's stammering apology: 'certain events...certain things...certain situations...certain accountants'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to apologize without naming what he actually did (kissed Oscar in front of the entire office)
jokes.punchline: His non-apology escalates through progressively specific but still vague categories until landing on 'certain accountants' — the most specific phrase that still avoids saying anything
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity of 'certain' (events → things → situations → accountants) is a well-constructed bit. Michael's commitment to vagueness while appearing to be confessing is very true to the character. The comedy comes from the structure of his evasion.

jokes.text: Andy tries to join the party planning committee; Angela: 'Never.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has just been warmly welcomed to the committee
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately tries to capitalize on the good vibes to join; Angela's single-word refusal ('Never') is instant, absolute, and utterly without compassion
jokes.explanation: The joke is entirely in the one-word delivery and its absoluteness. Angela's 'Never' doesn't invite discussion or give a reason — it's a verdict. The contrast with Oscar's warm welcome makes it land harder. High economy, high character integration.

jokes.text: Andy's response to a sales win: 'Child's play. Give me something hard to sell.'
jokes.setup: Michael praises Andy for selling two printers
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately dismisses the achievement and demands a greater challenge — performing competence rather than actually being competent
jokes.explanation: Functional character texture for Andy — the performative confidence is consistent with his character — but the joke doesn't have a sharp landing or subversion. It's setup without a real punchline.

jokes.text: Michael discovers his desk toys have not been arranged nicely; learns it was Dwight all along who arranged them
jokes.setup: Michael complains about the toys and plants, blaming the night cleaning crew
jokes.punchline: Pam reveals it was Dwight who brightened Michael's mornings by arranging his toys — a small, absurd act of devotion that Michael never knew about and now can never get back
jokes.explanation: A small, beautifully executed moment that retroactively enriches Dwight's character. The idea that Dwight quietly arranged Michael's toys every morning — a completely unnecessary act of service — is both funny and weirdly touching. The comedy comes from Michael's obliviousness and the absurdity of Dwight's devotion.

jokes.text: Michael uses 'feel ya, dawg' and then tries to explain that it means 'right on' — and his explanation gets increasingly muddled
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to seem culturally connected and relatable
jokes.punchline: His definition of 'feel ya, dawg' spirals into an inarticulate breakdown ('You are like... Pam is like...') that culminates in a satisfied 'Nailed it' with zero actual communication achieved
jokes.explanation: Standard Michael cringe bit — using slang and then being unable to explain it. 'Nailed it' as self-assessment after saying nothing coherent is a reliable Michael move but not an especially original execution here.

jokes.text: Michael confessional about Andy: 'Love that Andy, right? Solid fellow. Seems smart enough. Likes me a lot. A lot. Too much. Like a crazy person, a little.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving his assessment of Andy as a new team member
jokes.punchline: His praise degrades in real time from 'solid fellow' to 'too much, like a crazy person' — and the irony is that Michael has zero self-awareness that he is exactly the same kind of person
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes because of its layered irony. Michael — a man who craves approval to pathological extremes — is diagnosing Andy as 'a crazy person' for the same behavior. The real-time degradation of the assessment ('A lot. Too much. Like a crazy person, a little.') is perfectly structured. High character integration: this is only funny because we know Michael has zero self-insight. Earns its 8+ score.

jokes.text: Michael: 'He's always up in my bid-ness, which is Ebonics for being in my face and annoying the bejesus out of me.'
jokes.setup: Michael is using slang to sound relatable while complaining about Andy
jokes.punchline: He immediately provides a formal definition of 'bid-ness' as if he's a translator, which undercuts any authenticity and reveals he's performing familiarity with a culture he doesn't belong to
jokes.explanation: Competent Michael cringe beat. The parenthetical definition of his own slang is genuinely funny and in character. Slightly similar to the 'feel ya dawg' beat earlier in the episode, which reduces its freshness.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I don't understand how someone could have so little self-awareness.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just described Andy as a sycophantic people-pleaser who lacks social awareness
jokes.punchline: Michael Scott — the least self-aware character in the series — says this with complete sincerity and zero irony
jokes.explanation: Textbook irony executed with the precision the joke demands. The entire preceding confessional builds to this payoff, and it lands because the show trusts the audience completely — no nudge, no wink, just Michael saying the most ironic possible thing with total conviction. The character integration is a 9.5 because this joke ONLY works if you know Michael Scott. Among the episode's top three jokes.

jokes.text: Oscar's party planning: 'I really have no preference. We don't even have to have a party.'
jokes.setup: The office is planning an elaborate party to celebrate Oscar's return
jokes.punchline: Oscar — the person being celebrated — is completely indifferent to the party and would prefer they not bother; his understated deflection contrasts with Michael's enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Mild but effective — Oscar's complete lack of enthusiasm for his own celebration is a solid character beat. Not exceptional, but provides a grounded contrast to Michael's manic party planning.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Your Mexicanness is what defines you, to me, and I think we should celebrate Oscar's Mexicanity.'
jokes.setup: Michael just said Oscar's 'gayness does not define you'
jokes.punchline: He immediately replaces one stereotype with another, not recognizing the contradiction, and invents the word 'Mexicanity' to describe what he sees as the correct defining trait
jokes.explanation: Michael's inability to get out of his own way — replacing one problematic framework with another while congratulating himself — is peak Michael Scott. 'Mexicanity' is a great invented word that reveals his processing of identity. The structural joke (the immediate pivot from 'gayness doesn't define you' to 'your Mexicanness defines you') is very well-constructed.

jokes.text: Michael instructs Phyllis to 'find firecrackers and a chihuahua' for Oscar's Mexican-themed party
jokes.setup: Michael is planning what he thinks is a culturally appropriate celebration for Oscar
jokes.punchline: His idea of Mexican culture is so reductive and absurd that 'firecrackers and a chihuahua' is genuinely the best he can manage — and he says it with total conviction
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'a chihuahua' is what makes this joke work — not just stereotyped food or music, but a specific small dog as a cultural representative. The absurdity is well-targeted. The joke is uncomfortable in the right way for this show.

jokes.text: Michael asks Pam to get chimechangas from the frozen food section (mispronouncing chimichangas)
jokes.setup: Michael is building a list of authentic Mexican elements for Oscar's party
jokes.punchline: He pronounces 'chimichangas' as 'chimechangas,' adding mild malapropism to his existing cultural incompetence — and names Swanson (a deeply un-Mexican brand) as the source
jokes.explanation: Competent but not exceptional. The Swanson detail is good (frozen food brand as authentic Mexican cuisine source), but the mispronunciation is a thin joke compared to the surrounding material.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'Why don't you have me riding in on a donkey, into the office, like Pepe?' Michael: 'Ah, a burro, of course. If Oscar wants a donkey, let's get him one.'
jokes.setup: Oscar is sarcastically listing how stereotyped Michael's party is
jokes.punchline: Michael takes the sarcasm completely literally and enthusiastically agrees to obtain a donkey — and corrects Oscar's word choice while doing so, missing the entire point entirely
jokes.explanation: Perfect Michael Scott obliviousness. Oscar's sarcasm is obvious to everyone in the room except Michael, who not only takes it literally but actively corrects the vocabulary ('a burro, of course') — demonstrating he has both no irony detector AND unexpected niche knowledge about donkey terminology. The combination is very funny.

jokes.text: Dwight at a menial retail job: 'Need any help?' 'Oh, no thank you. I'm just looking.' 'Great. I will literally be standing right here if you need anything at all.'
jokes.setup: Dwight, recently the top salesman at a major paper company, is now doing a menial customer service job
jokes.punchline: His commitment to hovering over customers — 'literally standing right here' — suggests he's applying the same intense salesman energy to a low-stakes retail situation, and the customer's polite refusal has done nothing to deter him
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Dwight's post-Dunder Mifflin situation. His retail intensity mirrors his prior sales persona, and the customer's clear discomfort mirrors his usual effect on people. Solid situational comedy.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I think I could go for some tuna fish right about now. Got my rod here.'
jokes.setup: Andy calls Jim 'Large Tuna' and is now fishing for Jim's attention through an extended metaphor
jokes.punchline: He announces he has brought a rod to fish for Jim — the metaphor has become a committed bit that Andy is executing without any apparent awareness that it's unbearably weird
jokes.explanation: The 'fishing for tuna' metaphor is mildly amusing but somewhat played out by this point in the episode. It extends the 'Large Tuna' nickname without adding much new comedy. Functional but not elevated.

jokes.text: Jim to Pam: 'I'm the victim, okay? He's fishing for me.'
jokes.setup: Pam suggests Jim shouldn't encourage Andy's behavior
jokes.punchline: Jim reframes the situation as Andy being a predator and himself as prey, the reversal of the normal power dynamic is funny given Jim is physically and professionally the more dominant figure
jokes.explanation: Jim casting himself as the hapless victim being hunted by Andy is a fun character reversal. Jim is usually the instigator; here he's genuinely being victimized by someone who out-annoys him.

jokes.text: Jim explains he can't prank Andy because Dwight's inherited files are password-protected with different mythical creatures
jokes.setup: Jim is being asked to help prank Andy
jokes.punchline: His excuse is that he's busy cracking Dwight's mythical-creature password system — a detail that reveals the absurd extent of Dwight's paranoid security infrastructure even in his absence
jokes.explanation: A great background worldbuilding joke: Dwight set every client file with a different mythical creature password. The specificity ('different mythical creature' for each file) and the fact that this is presented as a serious workplace problem is very funny. High character integration for Dwight even in absentia.

jokes.text: Jim describes Andy: 'Who's that sportscaster that bit that lady? Marv something? Andy is like Marv something.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to articulate what's wrong with Andy
jokes.punchline: The most specific comparison he can make is to a sportscaster famous for a bizarre assault, and he can't even remember the name — using 'Marv something' as if this is sufficient specificity
jokes.explanation: The joke relies partly on audience knowledge of the Marv Albert incident, which was widely known in 2007. The half-remembered reference ('Marv something') is a nice touch suggesting Jim knows enough to make the comparison but doesn't consider Andy worth the research. Mildly funny, period-specific.

jokes.text: Ryan: 'Do you want to pull a prank on Andy?' Ryan: 'Not right now. But ask me again ten years ago.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to recruit Ryan for an Andy prank
jokes.punchline: Ryan declines with 'ask me again ten years ago' — a grammatically impossible but tonally perfect response suggesting he's now too corporate/serious to participate in pranks
jokes.explanation: Sharp, highly quotable line that perfectly captures Ryan's character arc — he's gone corporate and looks back on his temp-days humor as embarrassingly beneath him. 'Ten years ago' is an impossible timeline that makes perfect emotional sense: Ryan is so over it that he's retroactively uninterested. High economy, high character integration. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Jim: 'I liked you better as the temp.' Ryan: 'Me too.'
jokes.setup: Jim has just been rebuffed by the newly corporate Ryan
jokes.punchline: Ryan agrees that he liked himself better as the temp — a quiet admission that his corporate ascent has cost him something, delivered without sentiment
jokes.explanation: Two words from Ryan ('Me too.') that do extraordinary character work. The unexpected agreement transforms the insult into a melancholy moment of self-awareness — Ryan knows what he's become and doesn't fully approve. This is elevated comedy writing: funny on the surface, honest underneath. Economy score is very high. Earns its 8+ rating.

jokes.text: Montage: Phyllis says she and Dwight both have 'big personalities' and it was 'explosive' — then immediately pivots to weather small talk
jokes.setup: Phyllis is asked if she was close to Dwight
jokes.punchline: She claims a dramatic interpersonal dynamic ('big personalities, explosive') then immediately deflates into weather commentary — suggesting she actually has nothing to say about Dwight and this was all posturing
jokes.explanation: Good Phyllis character beat. The self-aggrandizement about her 'big personality' followed immediately by banal weather small talk is a nice structural joke about people who overestimate their own importance in others' stories.

jokes.text: Dwight at the competitor: 'I have snow tires and chains. Plus exceptional hand-eye coordination.'
jokes.setup: A coworker makes a casual remark about the weather and commute
jokes.punchline: Dwight responds with a prepared, itemized account of his weather-related driving qualifications — 'snow tires and chains' are reasonable, but 'exceptional hand-eye coordination' as a weather asset is the absurdist overstep
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight: escalating a mundane social exchange into a declaration of personal superiority. The addition of 'exceptional hand-eye coordination' to a list of car equipment is the absurdist step that characterizes him perfectly — he counts personal physical attributes as driving equipment.

jokes.text: Dwight at his retail job interview: 'Have you heard of paper?' after interviewer says she never heard of Dunder-Mifflin
jokes.setup: A potential employer admits unfamiliarity with Dunder-Mifflin; Dwight tries to establish the company's credibility
jokes.punchline: Rather than explain further, Dwight responds 'Have you heard of paper?' — an absurdist appeal to the most fundamental possible product category, delivered with genuine contempt
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight joke. The logic is genuinely sound from Dwight's perspective — if you know paper, you know Dunder-Mifflin — but delivered as a devastating comeback to someone he's trying to impress. The contempt for a potential employer while simultaneously needing their approval is perfect Dwight. Highly quotable, economical, character-specific. Earns its 8+ rating.

jokes.text: Dwight confessional: 'I don't like him, his giant head, or his beady little eyes. That's all I got to say on the matter.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has bombed a job interview due to his contemptuous attitude
jokes.punchline: His verdict on the interviewer dismisses the man's credentials entirely in favor of physical grievances — and 'that's all I got to say on the matter' signals a finality that leaves no room for reflection
jokes.explanation: Dwight's grievances are entirely physical and delivered with judicial gravity. 'Giant head' and 'beady little eyes' as the definitive objections, sealed with 'that's all I got to say on the matter,' is a great Dwight non sequitur. The formality of the closing clause is the joke.

jokes.text: Dwight sings the Cranberries' 'Zombie' to himself while working at retail
jokes.setup: Dwight is doing a mundane retail task
jokes.punchline: He's singing an aggressively dramatic alt-rock song to himself — the intensity of the song ('In your head! Zombie! Zombie!') is wildly mismatched with the mundane setting, and is almost certainly performed with total commitment
jokes.explanation: A good visual moment that works mainly through Dwight's commitment and the absurd song choice. 'Zombie' as Dwight's retail soundtrack is funny but the joke is situational — it doesn't have much structure beyond the incongruity.

jokes.text: Andy realizes his cell phone is missing and searches desperately while Jim and Pam play innocent
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam have hidden Andy's phone; Andy calls it repeatedly and can hear it but can't find it
jokes.punchline: Andy becomes increasingly frantic ('Where is my freaking phone?') as the sound taunts him from an unknown location — the prank has graduated from mild to full cringe spiral
jokes.explanation: The prank works partly as a callback to Andy's obsessive ringtone crafting — his vanity project becomes his torment. The escalation of Andy's distress over a missing phone is good cringe territory, though the extended search sequence dilutes the comedy somewhat.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Large Tuna, have you seen my cell phone device?'
jokes.setup: Andy is looking for his phone, unaware it's been hidden as a prank
jokes.punchline: 'Cell phone device' — Andy's redundant formulation, as if clarifying what kind of phone (a cell phone, not a landline phone, not a smoke-signal device), combined with 'Large Tuna' as his nickname for Jim
jokes.explanation: 'Cell phone device' is a redundancy that reveals Andy's slightly-off relationship with casual language. 'Large Tuna' continues the nickname running gag. Works as texture rather than a standalone joke.

jokes.text: The phone is heard ringing from inside the ceiling; Andy: 'Maybe it's in the ceiling.' Jim: 'You know what? Maybe YOU'RE in the ceiling.'
jokes.setup: Andy deduces his phone might be in the ceiling tiles based on where the sound is coming from
jokes.punchline: Jim — presumably the person who put it there — responds with an irritated nonsense retort ('Maybe YOU'RE in the ceiling') that is both a deflection and an absurdly bad comeback, delivered with the confidence of someone hiding something
jokes.explanation: Jim's nonsensical deflection ('Maybe YOU'RE in the ceiling') is funny because it's such a transparently bad cover — it's not even a clever misdirection, just absurdist noise from someone who accidentally got caught. The panic underneath the confident delivery is the joke.

jokes.text: The phone is hidden in the ceiling; Angela calls it to keep it ringing; she says 'Is everything okay? No.' — a terse exchange that reveals her participation in the prank
jokes.setup: Angela, of all people, is the one keeping the phone ringing to sustain the prank
jokes.punchline: Angela — uptight, disapproving, rules-obsessed Angela — is participating in workplace mischief, her only line being the flat, clipped 'Is everything okay? No.' suggesting she enjoys this
jokes.explanation: Angela being in on the prank and being clearly okay with it is a great character reveal. Her enjoyment of Andy's suffering is entirely consistent with her disdain for him (established by 'Never' earlier). Her flat 'Is everything okay? No.' is a perfectly Angela response.

jokes.text: Andy accuses Phyllis: 'I don't trust you, Phyllis.'
jokes.setup: Andy is accusing everyone in the office of stealing his phone
jokes.punchline: His specific targeting of Phyllis — the least likely phone thief — reveals his paranoia has become irrational, and Phyllis's reaction (presumably bemused indifference) amplifies the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Mild cringe beat. Andy accusing specific innocent people is a reasonable escalation of the prank sequence but this particular beat doesn't have a strong punchline — it relies on Phyllis's presumably baffled reaction which we can only infer.

jokes.text: Angela's confessional: reveals Dwight was late because he drove to New York to deliver tax forms Angela forgot to send — but immediately blames Kevin for not reminding her
jokes.setup: Angela is explaining why she's going to help bring Dwight back
jokes.punchline: Her confession of guilt immediately offloads the blame onto Kevin ('Though to be fair, Kevin never reminded me') — she's incapable of accepting responsibility even when she's theoretically being magnanimous
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed character moment. Angela's partial confession undermined by an immediate blame shift is very true to her character. The specificity of blaming Kevin for not reminding her of her own responsibility is funny and sharp.

jokes.text: Angela: 'Dwight loves this company. Do you think that anyone else out there would've driven to corporate for you? None of them. Especially not Andy.'
jokes.setup: Angela is making the case for Dwight's return to Michael
jokes.punchline: 'Especially not Andy' — a targeted aside that reveals Angela's already-formed contempt for the replacement, dropped in with complete certainty
jokes.explanation: The 'especially not Andy' addition is the joke — unprompted, specific, and delivered as settled fact. Angela's contempt for Andy is established efficiently without requiring elaboration.

jokes.text: Michael's Saturday plan monologue: 'you, me, bar, beers, buzzed. Wings, shots, drunk. Waitresses, hot. Football, Cornell/Hofstra, slaughter. Then quick nap at my place, and we hit the tiz-own.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to make plans with Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael delivers a Saturday itinerary in shorthand telegraphese that escalates from plausible ('beers') to bizarre ('quick nap at my place') to made-up slang ('tiz-own'), all delivered as if this is an irresistible offer
jokes.explanation: The compressed, staccato delivery style of the plan is a great comedic format — it reads like a sports broadcast treating a casual hangout as a mission. 'Tiz-own' as a finale, 'quick nap at my place' as a middle item, and 'Cornell/Hofstra, slaughter' as a football plan that acknowledges one team will be destroyed are all individually funny. 'Waitresses, hot' is a Michael Scott observation delivered completely without irony.

jokes.text: Andy, after being told to stop, retreats with: 'Sorry I annoyed you with my friendship.'
jokes.setup: Michael has finally told Andy to stop his relentless sucking-up
jokes.punchline: Andy frames his annoyance as an act of friendship — the passive-aggressive framing redefines his pathological behavior as a gift that Michael is ungrateful for
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and earns its score. 'Sorry I annoyed you with my friendship' is a perfectly constructed passive-aggressive non-apology that works as a joke, as a character revelation, and as a quotable line that extends beyond context. The framing of exhausting needy behavior as 'friendship' being rejected is both funny and a little sad. High quotability — this line has real cultural stickiness.

jokes.text: Andy's overwrought speech about the phone prank: 'Here's a little newsflash. It's not funny. In fact, it's pretty freakin' unfunny.'
jokes.setup: Andy has found his phone in the ceiling and is now addressing the office
jokes.punchline: His rage at a minor prank is wildly disproportionate, and his official verdict of 'pretty freakin' unfunny' is delivered with the gravity of a legal ruling — the overreaction is funnier than the prank itself
jokes.explanation: The overreaction is the joke. Andy's prosecutorial tone about office pranks signals that something is off with him — his anger management issues are beginning to show, which makes this beat both funny and a hint at things to come. 'Pretty freakin' unfunny' as a formal verdict is nicely absurd.

jokes.text: Andy's confessional after his office speech: 'That was an overreaction.'
jokes.setup: Andy just delivered a theatrical address to the entire office about the unfunniness of phone pranks
jokes.punchline: In the talking head, he concedes with remarkable calm that it was an overreaction — showing brief self-awareness that immediately disappears as he moves on
jokes.explanation: The calm, matter-of-fact delivery of 'That was an overreaction' is a perfect talking-head beat. Andy can step back and see the overreaction but treats it as a closed matter — no guilt, no plan to change, just an observation. The disconnect between awareness and behavior is the joke.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional non-advice: 'Just go with the copy paper. It's your funeral.'
jokes.setup: Someone (inferred from context) is asking Michael for business advice or product guidance
jokes.punchline: Michael's advice is a shrug followed by a death threat metaphor — completely unhelpful and weirdly fatalistic for someone who sees himself as a mentor
jokes.explanation: Mild background joke. The 'it's your funeral' as a paper recommendation is a good Michael line but appears without much setup or context in the transcript, making it harder to fully assess. Competent but not a standout.

jokes.text: Michael to Dwight: 'It takes a big man to admit his mistake. And I am that big man.'
jokes.setup: Michael is attempting a heartfelt reconciliation with Dwight
jokes.punchline: He begins with a proverb about humility then immediately inserts himself as the exemplar of that proverb — the self-congratulation undermines the humility he's claiming to demonstrate
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott structure: cliché about virtuous quality, immediately self-applied. The joke is in the gap between the humility the proverb espouses and the pride with which Michael claims it. It's a repeating Michael pattern but executed well here.

jokes.text: Michael to Dwight: 'It takes a big man to admit his mistake. And I am that big man.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to bring Dwight back by apologizing
jokes.punchline: Michael uses the humble 'big man' framework — a cliché about emotional maturity — and immediately, reflexively applies it to himself, making the apology about his own greatness
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael: co-opting a sentiment about humility to make a claim about his own bigness. 'And I am that big man' — the self-compliment embedded in the apology — is perfectly Michael. He can't not make it about himself even when he's trying to be selfless.

jokes.text: Dwight on his new workplace: 'The boss isn't funny. I don't get to wear my ties.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks how Dwight's new job is treating him
jokes.punchline: Dwight's chief complaints about his new job are (1) boss's lack of humor and (2) tie restrictions — revealing that what he values about work is incredibly specific and also somewhat unhinged as priorities
jokes.explanation: The pairing of a legitimate grievance (humor) with a highly specific personal one (ties) is a Dwight classic. What makes it funny is the equivalence — both complaints are delivered as equally serious. The ties are clearly a significant part of Dwight's identity and losing them is a genuine wound.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I don't want to do your laundry anymore.' Dwight: 'We can talk about that.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to persuade Dwight to return; Dwight is negotiating
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Michael does Dwight's laundry — a deeply odd domestic arrangement — is slipped in as a negotiating point, with Dwight treating it as a legitimate contract term
jokes.explanation: The Michael-Dwight relationship has always had an unusual power dynamic, but the laundry revelation is a new and funny detail. Michael doing Dwight's laundry suggests their relationship has some deeply weird domestic elements — and 'we can talk about that' treats it as a negotiable term in an employment contract. Absurdist and character-specific.

jokes.text: Dwight crashes through ceiling tiles pursuing his phone — 'That's half-inch drywall. I think we broke his brain.'
jokes.setup: Jim or Pam observes Dwight's reaction to the revelation/prank
jokes.punchline: The physical comedy of Dwight damaging the ceiling combined with the clinical assessment 'I think we broke his brain' — treating Dwight's frantic behavior as a technical malfunction
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy is a good escalation of the ceiling phone prank (which was originally aimed at Andy, not Dwight). 'We broke his brain' as a clinical diagnosis of Dwight's reaction is a nice line. The slapstick is more effective than most of this type because it's grounded in character (Dwight's intensity leading to property damage).

jokes.text: Andy's callback: 'It's not freaking funny.' — echoing his earlier speech, now that someone else is getting pranked
jokes.setup: Andy made a big speech about pranks being 'not funny' when he was the victim
jokes.punchline: Now that Dwight is the prank victim, Andy repeats the same line — except now his complaint is about a prank that isn't even aimed at him, suggesting he's still performing the victim role he established earlier
jokes.explanation: Good callback that gets extra mileage from Andy's earlier outrage. The joke is that Andy has now self-appointed as the office prank grievance spokesperson, applying his verdict to a situation that doesn't involve him.

jokes.text: Oscar: 'Actually, yeah. I didn't think I would... but it turned out great.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks if Oscar is enjoying his stereotyped Mexican fiesta
jokes.punchline: Oscar — who spent the entire party planning sequence appalled by Michael's ethnic reductiveness — admits he's actually having a good time, deflating the expected outcome
jokes.explanation: The subversion of expectations — the party Oscar wanted no part of ended up being genuinely enjoyable — is a nice comedic reversal and a small grace note for Michael's chaotic good. The 'I didn't think I would' admission against expectation is the joke.

jokes.text: Michael introduces Dwight to the office; then: 'Okay, Dwight, you can let go of her hand. You're going to break it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is welcomed back to the office; the audience infers he grabs someone's hand
jokes.punchline: Dwight's grip on Angela's hand is so intense that Michael has to physically intervene — Dwight's emotion translating into a vice-like handshake is completely in character
jokes.explanation: Dwight experiencing overwhelming emotion and expressing it through crushing a hand is a great physical comedy beat that's entirely consistent with his character. The matter-of-fact intervention ('you're going to break it') from Michael is the right delivery.

jokes.text: Jim asks Dwight: 'Do you still have feelings for her?' — long pause — Dwight: 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Dwight are observing the party; the Dwight-Angela relationship has been a running thread
jokes.punchline: After a significant pause, Dwight admits feelings for Angela with total honesty and no deflection — the sincerity is both touching and funny because Dwight never does sincerity without it being slightly awkward
jokes.explanation: The pause before 'Yes' does the comedic and emotional work simultaneously. Dwight's unguarded honesty is both funny (because it's Dwight) and genuinely affecting. The economy of the exchange is very high — everything in the silence and the single word. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing where this relationship goes.

jokes.text: Michael's closing confessional: 'I don't want somebody sucking up to me because they think I'm going to help their career. I want them sucking up to me because they genuinely love me.'
jokes.setup: Michael claims to have learned something from the Andy experience
jokes.punchline: His 'lesson' is that he wants GENUINE sycophancy, not strategic sycophancy — the distinction is absurd because he can't conceive of people not wanting to suck up to him at all; the question is only about motivation
jokes.explanation: One of the series' great Michael Scott lines and the episode's strongest closing joke. The genius is in the structure: Michael frames this as a lesson in discernment ('I can tell authentic from fake sycophancy') but the actual content reveals he has zero desire to not be sucked up to — he just wants it to be real. The assumption that love = sucking up is deeply Michaelian. The parallel structure ('not because they think... because they genuinely love me') is elegant. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, and earns an 8+ score by these criteria.

tmdb_overview: Since Dwight's departure, Andy had been clinging to Michael. Andy's antics had been wearing very thin on his co-workers. In fact, Andy left Jim actually wishing Dwight would come back.
